patterns.name: Basic SELECT and filtering
patterns.problem: List rows/columns that satisfy simple conditions.
patterns.template:
SELECT `Company`, `City`
FROM customers
WHERE `State/Province` = 'WA'
  AND `City` <> 'Seattle';
patterns.explanation: WHERE filters rows before any grouping. Quote identifiers that contain spaces or "/" with backticks; string literals use single quotes.
mistakes: Using double quotes for strings (MySQL may read them as identifiers in ANSI mode).
Forgetting backticks around `Last Name`.
Using = NULL instead of IS NULL.
notWhen: When the condition needs an aggregate: use HAVING.

patterns.name: ORDER BY and LIMIT
patterns.problem: Sort the result and keep only the first rows.
patterns.template:
SELECT *
FROM products
ORDER BY `List Price` DESC, ID
LIMIT 5;
patterns.explanation: ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT cuts after sorting. Add a tie-breaker column so the output is deterministic.
mistakes: LIMIT without ORDER BY gives arbitrary rows.
Ties at the cut-off are silently dropped.
Writing ORDER BY a DESC, b when both must be DESC.
notWhen: When ties must all be returned: use a subquery on the threshold value or RANK()/DENSE_RANK().

patterns.name: DISTINCT / unique values
patterns.problem: Return each value only once.
patterns.template:
SELECT DISTINCT `Ship Country/Region`
FROM orders;
patterns.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows (whole row, not first column). COUNT(DISTINCT x) counts different values of x.
mistakes: Believing DISTINCT applies to only the first selected column.
Using DISTINCT to hide a wrong join that multiplies rows.
COUNT(DISTINCT a, b) is not the same as two separate counts.
notWhen: When per-group aggregates are also needed: use GROUP BY.

patterns.name: Aggregate functions
patterns.problem: COUNT / SUM / AVG / MIN / MAX over a set of rows.
patterns.explanation: Aggregates collapse rows into one value; NULLs are ignored by every aggregate except COUNT(*).
mistakes: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col): the latter skips NULLs.
AVG over a column with NULLs ignores them (not treated as 0).
Mixing non-aggregated columns without GROUP BY.
notWhen: When a value per group is needed: add GROUP BY.

patterns.name: GROUP BY and HAVING
patterns.problem: Aggregate per group and filter on the aggregate.
patterns.template:
SELECT `Customer ID`, COUNT(*) AS n_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY `Customer ID`
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
patterns.explanation: GROUP BY forms groups; HAVING filters groups after aggregation (WHERE filters rows before). More than N => > N, at least N => >= N.
mistakes: Putting an aggregate in WHERE.
> vs >= (more than vs at least).
Grouping by a name that is not unique (group by the ID too).
Selecting columns that are not in GROUP BY.
notWhen: When filtering on a plain column: use WHERE (cheaper).

patterns.name: INNER JOIN
patterns.problem: Combine rows from related tables; only matching rows survive.
patterns.explanation: JOIN ... ON links the foreign key to the primary key. Rows without a partner are dropped.
mistakes: Missing ON clause (cartesian product).
Joining on the wrong key (the dump declares no FK constraints).
Fan-out: joining one-to-many then summing a parent column.
notWhen: When unmatched rows must be kept: LEFT JOIN.

patterns.name: LEFT JOIN (keep unmatched)
patterns.problem: Keep all rows of the left table even without a match.
patterns.template:
SELECT c.ID, c.`Company`, COUNT(o.`Order ID`) AS n_orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Customer ID` = c.ID
GROUP BY c.ID, c.`Company`;
patterns.explanation: Unmatched left rows get NULLs on the right. COUNT(right.key) gives 0 for them; COUNT(*) would give 1.
mistakes: Filtering the right table in WHERE turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN (put the condition in ON).
COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(right.col).
notWhen: When only matching rows are wanted: INNER JOIN.

patterns.name: Subquery (scalar / derived table)
patterns.problem: Use the result of one query inside another.
patterns.explanation: A scalar subquery returns one value; a derived table in FROM needs an alias.
mistakes: Scalar subquery returning more than one row (error).
Missing alias on derived table.
notWhen: When it can be a plain join without losing clarity.

patterns.name: EXISTS
patterns.problem: Keep rows for which a related row exists.
patterns.explanation: EXISTS stops at the first match and is NULL-safe; no duplicates from the outer table.
mistakes: Forgetting the correlation condition (EXISTS always true).
notWhen: When you need columns from the inner table: JOIN.

patterns.name: NOT EXISTS / anti-join
patterns.problem: Keep rows with NO related row.
patterns.explanation: NOT EXISTS is the safe anti-join. Equivalent: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL.
mistakes: NOT IN with a subquery that returns NULL gives an empty result.
Inner join + <> does NOT express "never".

patterns.name: IN / NOT IN
patterns.problem: Membership test against a list or subquery.
patterns.explanation: IN tests against a set. NOT IN is dangerous when the set contains NULL (comparison becomes UNKNOWN for every row).
mistakes: NOT IN + NULL in subquery => no rows.
Large IN-lists are slow compared with a join.
notWhen: Negation with nullable columns: use NOT EXISTS.

patterns.name: Correlated subquery
patterns.problem: Inner query references the outer row.
patterns.explanation: The inner query runs per outer row (logically). Typical for "greater than the average of its own group".
mistakes: Using the same alias in both levels.
Forgetting the correlation => global average.
notWhen: Big tables: a window function or a join to a grouped derived table is usually faster.

patterns.name: SELF JOIN
patterns.problem: Join a table to itself to compare rows or form pairs.
patterns.template:
SELECT a.`Product ID` AS p1, b.`Product ID` AS p2, COUNT(*) AS together
FROM `order details` AS a
JOIN `order details` AS b ON a.`Order ID` = b.`Order ID` AND a.`Product ID` < b.`Product ID`
GROUP BY a.`Product ID`, b.`Product ID`
ORDER BY together DESC;
patterns.explanation: Two aliases of one table. Use < (not <>) on the key so each unordered pair appears once and no row pairs with itself.
mistakes: <> returns each pair twice.
Missing the self-pair exclusion.

patterns.name: Conditional aggregation
patterns.problem: Several filtered aggregates in one pass (pivot-like).
patterns.template:
SELECT `Employee ID`,
       SUM(CASE WHEN `Shipped Date` IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS not_shipped,
       SUM(CASE WHEN `Shipped Date` IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shipped
FROM orders
GROUP BY `Employee ID`;
patterns.explanation: SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN x ELSE 0 END) or COUNT(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END) counts/sums only matching rows per group.
mistakes: COUNT(CASE ... ELSE 0 END) counts every row (0 is not NULL).
Using WHERE would filter away the other categories.

patterns.name: Date manipulation
patterns.problem: Filter or group by year/month/day.
patterns.template:
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(`Order Date`, '%Y-%m') AS ym, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
WHERE `Order Date` >= '2006-01-01' AND `Order Date` < '2007-01-01'
GROUP BY ym;
patterns.explanation: Prefer a half-open range (>= start AND < next start) over YEAR(col)=2006: it can use an index. DATE_FORMAT builds YYYY-MM keys.
mistakes: BETWEEN with datetime misses the last day after 00:00:00.
Functions on the column disable index use.
Mixing %m (month) and %i (minute) in DATE_FORMAT.

patterns.name: Ranking and Top-N (incl. Nth)
patterns.problem: Top N rows, Nth highest, ranking with or without ties.
patterns.template:
SELECT *
FROM orders
ORDER BY `Shipping Fee` DESC, `Order ID`
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 5;  -- 6th..8th row

-- ties-aware: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY `Shipping Fee` DESC) BETWEEN 6 AND 8
patterns.explanation: LIMIT/OFFSET ranks by ROW position; RANK/DENSE_RANK rank by VALUE and treat equal values as tied. Decide which one the question means.
mistakes: OFFSET is 0-based: 6th row => OFFSET 5.
Ignoring ties.
Nth highest value vs Nth row.

patterns.name: Multiple-table aggregation
patterns.problem: Join several tables then aggregate.
patterns.template:
SELECT c.ID, c.`Company`, SUM(od.`Unit Price` * od.Quantity) AS total
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.`Customer ID` = c.ID
JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID`
GROUP BY c.ID, c.`Company`;
patterns.explanation: Follow the key chain customers -> orders -> order details -> products. Aggregate at the end, group by the entity key.
mistakes: Summing an orders column after joining order details (fan-out, double counting).
Grouping by name only.

patterns.name: Query optimization
patterns.problem: Make a query use indexes and read less data.
patterns.explanation: Avoid SELECT *, avoid functions on indexed columns, filter early, index filter/join/sort columns, check with EXPLAIN.
mistakes: Index on a column wrapped in a function is unused.
Leading-wildcard LIKE is not index-friendly.

patterns.name: NULL handling
patterns.problem: Missing values in filters, aggregates and comparisons.
patterns.explanation: NULL = anything is UNKNOWN. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, COALESCE for defaults; aggregates skip NULLs.
mistakes: col = NULL never matches.
<> excludes NULL rows silently.
NOT IN with NULL.

patterns.name: Relational division
patterns.problem: Entities related to ALL members of a set.
patterns.template:
SELECT o.`Customer ID`
FROM orders AS o
JOIN `order details` AS od ON od.`Order ID` = o.`Order ID`
JOIN products AS p ON p.ID = od.`Product ID`
WHERE p.Category = 'Beverages'
GROUP BY o.`Customer ID`
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.ID) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products WHERE Category = 'Beverages');
patterns.explanation: Count the distinct members each entity covers and compare with the total number of members. Alternative: double NOT EXISTS.
mistakes: COUNT without DISTINCT.
Comparing against a count that was not restricted to the same subset.

patterns.name: Computed columns and ratios
patterns.problem: Derived expressions, ratios, rounding, percentages.
patterns.explanation: Column aliases cannot be used in WHERE; repeat the expression or use HAVING / a derived table. 50% => 0.5.
mistakes: Alias in WHERE.
Percent written as 50 instead of 0.5.
Division by zero yields NULL in MySQL.

patterns.name: ALL / ANY comparison
patterns.problem: Compare with every / at least one value of a subquery.
patterns.template:
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE `List Price` > ALL (SELECT `List Price` FROM products WHERE Category = 'Beverages');
patterns.explanation: > ALL = greater than the maximum; > ANY = greater than the minimum. Equivalent to comparing with MAX()/MIN().
mistakes: Mixing up ALL and ANY.
ALL over an empty set is true.

patterns.name: UNION / UNION ALL
patterns.problem: Stack results of several queries.
patterns.explanation: UNION removes duplicates (extra sort/dedup); UNION ALL keeps all rows and is faster. Column counts and types must match.
mistakes: UNION when duplicates are wanted.
Different column order between branches.

patterns.name: String functions
patterns.problem: Build or split text: CONCAT, UPPER, REPLACE, SUBSTRING_INDEX, LIKE.
patterns.template:
SELECT CONCAT(`First Name`, ' ', UPPER(`Last Name`)) AS full_name,
       SUBSTRING_INDEX(`E-mail Address`, '@', -1) AS domain,
       REPLACE(`Job Title`, 'Sales ', '') AS short_title
FROM employees;
patterns.explanation: CONCAT returns NULL if any argument is NULL (CONCAT_WS skips NULLs). SUBSTRING_INDEX(s, sep, n): n>0 text before the nth separator, n<0 text after the nth separator from the right. LENGTH counts bytes, CHAR_LENGTH counts characters.
mistakes: Forgetting the space/trailing separator in REPLACE.
LENGTH vs CHAR_LENGTH.
LIKE wildcards: % any string, _ one character.

entries.question: For each customer, shipper and product category combination, return IDs, company names and discounted line revenue rounded to cents.
entries.answer: SELECT customer.ID, customer.Company, shipper.ID, shipper.Company, product.Category, ROUND(SUM(line.Quantity*line.`Unit Price`*(1-line.Discount)),2) FROM customers customer JOIN orders ord ON ord.`Customer ID`=customer.ID JOIN shippers shipper ON shipper.ID=ord.`Shipper ID` JOIN `order details` line ON line.`Order ID`=ord.`Order ID` JOIN products product ON product.ID=line.`Product ID` GROUP BY customer.ID, customer.Company, shipper.ID, shipper.Company, product.Category;
entries.alternative: WITH category_sales AS (SELECT ord.`Customer ID` customer_id, ord.`Shipper ID` shipper_id, product.Category, SUM(line.Quantity*line.`Unit Price`*(1-line.Discount)) revenue FROM orders ord JOIN `order details` line ON line.`Order ID`=ord.`Order ID` JOIN products product ON product.ID=line.`Product ID` GROUP BY ord.`Customer ID`, ord.`Shipper ID`, product.Category) SELECT customer.ID, customer.Company, shipper.ID, shipper.Company, category_sales.Category, ROUND(category_sales.revenue,2) FROM category_sales JOIN customers customer ON customer.ID=category_sales.customer_id JOIN shippers shipper ON shipper.ID=category_sales.shipper_id;
entries.explanation: Revenue uses actual line prices after Discount; shipping and taxes are excluded. Only existing customer/assigned-shipper/category combinations appear; aggregate before joining descriptive entities in the alternative.
